content: 1. Combining multiple specimen types for diagnosing pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) in children has been evaluated. Limited data suggest that non-invasive specimens, such as stool or nasopharyngeal aspirates, perform comparably to traditional gastric aspirates or induced sputum specimens. 2. Operational and qualitative research is needed to determine the best methods for less invasive specimen collection in children. This includes studies on nasopharyngeal aspiration using suction methods suitable for low-resource settings, research on stool as a diagnostic specimen in treatment decision algorithms, and defining laboratory protocols that balance ease of implementation with diagnostic performance. 3. The identification, evaluation, and validation of hostand pathogen-associated biomarkers in pediatric populations are critical. These biomarkers could serve as novel diagnostic tools for TB infection, disease progression risk, and treatment response, ideally using non-invasive samples and point-of-care testing. 4. Efforts to optimize the current microbiological reference standard include improving and harmonizing specimen collection, supporting laboratory research to enhance specimen processing for better diagnostic yield, and improving phenotypic and genotypic drug-susceptibility testing, including on stool samples. 5. Qualitative research is required to address equity, acceptability, and feasibility of diagnostic approaches, including specimen types and diagnostic tools. 6. A four-month treatment regimen for children and adolescents with non-severe, drug-susceptible TB is being explored. Stronger evidence is needed to support the feasibility of diagnosing non-severe TB in settings without access to diagnostic tools, particularly chest X-rays (CXR). 7. The societal costs of implementing shorter treatment regimens for drug-susceptible TB, including direct and indirect costs such as transportation and loss of family income, need to be evaluated. 8. Automated software for CXR interpretation, including differentiation between severe and non-severe intrathoracic TB in children, is under consideration. 9. For multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in children, treatment outcomes with shorter and longer all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline are being studied. Research is also focused on optimizing bedaquiline dosing, understanding resistance mechanisms, and evaluating the cost-effectiveness of its use in children. 10. Studies are exploring the safety and pharmacokinetics (PK) of bedaquiline and delamanid in children, including their concomitant use, and the optimal duration of treatment. Long-term safety data on delamanid, particularly regarding neuropsychiatric side effects, are also being collected. 11. Research on TB meningitis (TBM) in children includes comparative efficacy and safety of short intensive versus standard treatment regimens, dosing for alternative regimens, equitable access to medicines, and cost-effectiveness of shorter regimens. The feasibility and acceptability of these regimens, as well as the sequelae of TBM and quality of life post-treatment, are being studied. 12. Decentralization of TB services for children and adolescents with TB symptoms or exposure is being evaluated for cost-effectiveness, health equity impact, and feasibility. Family-centered, integrated services are being assessed for their implementation, costs, and outcomes, including TB preventive treatment (TPT) initiation, diagnosis rates, treatment completion, and clinical outcomes. 13. Research priorities include addressing under-diagnosis and over-diagnosis of TB in children, community perceptions of TB care, and the quality of TB diagnosis.
